sentences.text:
This petition under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure has been filed by the petitioners seeking quashment of the FIR bearing Crime No.193/2020, registered at Police Station Badoni,
District Datia, on 15.8.2020, for offences punishable under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471 of IPC, and all other consequential proceedings arising therefrom.

2. As per the prosecution case, on 14.06.2020, the complainant submitted an application at Police Station Badoni, alleging that land measuring 30x30 sq. ft., situated at Moja, Badoni within Nagar Panchayat Badoni, was allotted in the name of Vishvajeet Singh by the Nagar Panchayat Badoni vide its resolution dated 27.01.2009, along with a No Objection Certificate provided by the Panchayat on the same date.

However, the accused persons, by applying underhanded means, got a sale deed NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26030 2 MCRC-37168-2021 registered on 13.11.2019,
wherein the present applicant projected himself as the seller and the co-accused as the buyers.
They had no right to sell the land belonging to the complainant and his family.
After inquiry, an FIR was registered at Crime No. 193/2020 for the offences punishable under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the IPC.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner argued that from the contents of the FIR, no offence of cheating or forgery is prima facie made out against the petitioners.

The land in question does not, in Azad Khan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21282029/
1 any way, belong to the complainant.

sentences.text: The Village Panchayat Badoni, Datia, by its resolution and order dated 01.12.2004, allotted the said land to one Anish Khan.
After the said order, Anish Khan also paid the premium for the land, as evidenced by receipt no. 71 dated 01.12.2004.
After fulfillment of all the necessary requirements and formalities, the office of Village Panchayat Badoni Khurd issued an ownership certificate in favour of Anish Khan on 10.12.2004.

It is submitted by learned counsel that, after the allotment of the land in favour of Anish Khan, he acquired possession of the same and, thereafter, by a registered sale deed dated 25.02.2005, Anish Khan sold the land to petitioner no. 1.
In the sale deed, it is clearly mentioned that the said land was allotted to Anish Khan by the Panchayat.

It is further alleges that the ownership certificate dated 10.12.2004, issued by Village Panchayat Badoni Khurd in favour of Anish Khan, is part of the sale deed and is still available in the office of the Registrar of Property, Datia.

Learned counsel further submitted that as petitioner no. 1 derived perfect title over the land in question through the sale deed dated 25.02.2005, he had full right and title over the said land NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:26030 3 MCRC-37168-2021 and, by exercising those rights, sold the land to petitioner no. 2 by a sale deed dated 18.11.2019.
The rights and title of petitioner no. 1 over the land in question are unquestionable; therefore, the allegations levelled in the application by respondent no. 2 are uncalled for.
It is thus submitted that the dispute between the parties is essentially civil in nature, but has been maliciously given a criminal colour to exert undue pressure upon the petitioners.
4. Per contra, learned counsel for respondents opposed the petition and prays for its rejection.

It s argued that from the surrounding circumstances, the presence of mens rea is clearly established,
which is a necessary ingredient for constituting the offence under Section 420 IPC.
It is further submitted that charges have already been framed against the petitioners, and the same have not been challenged.

5. Heard counsel for the parties and perused the record.
6.
Before proceeding further, it would be appropriate to reproduce the relevant provisions of law.

7. Section 420, Indian Penal Code (Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property):
"Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine."
8. Section 467, Indian Penal Code (Forgery of valuable security, will, etc.):

9. Section 468, Indian Penal Code (Forgery for purpose of cheating).
--
Whoever commits forgery, intending that the document or electronic record forged shall be used for the purpose of cheating, shall be punished with imprisonment of either de-scription for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
10. Section 471, Indian Penal Code (Using as genuine a forged document or electronic record).--

Whoever fraudulently or dishonestly uses as genuine any document or electronic record which he knows or has reason to believe to be a forged document or electronic record, shall be punished in the same manner as if he had forged such document or electronic record.

11. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of International Advanced Research Centre For Powder Metallurgy and New Materials (ARCI) & Ors. v. Nimra Cerglass Technics Private Limited and Anr.
reported in (2016) 1 SCC 348 while interpreting the definition of cheating has laid down the law as under :-
"15.

sentences.text:
The essential ingredients to attract Section 420 I.P.C. are: (i) NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26030 5 MCRC-37168-2021 cheating; (ii)
dishonest inducement to deliver property or to make, alter or destroy any valuable security or anything which is sealed or signed or is capable of being converted into a valuable security and (iii) mens rea of the accused at the time of making the inducement.
The making of a false representation is one of the essential ingredients to constitute the offence of cheating under Section 420 I.P.C.

In order to bring a case for the offence of cheating, it is not merely sufficient to prove that a false representation had been made, but, it is further necessary to prove that the representation was false to the knowledge of the accused and was made in order to deceive the complainant.
16. Distinction between mere breach of contract and the cheating would depend upon the intention of the accused at the time of alleged inducement.

If it is established that the intention of the accused was dishonest at the very time when he made a 1 Page 12 promise and entered into a transaction with the complainant to part with his property or money, then the liability is criminal and the accused is guilty of the Azad Khan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 8 October, 2025

On the other hand, if all that is established that a representation made by the accused has subsequently not been kept, criminal liability cannot be foisted on the accused and the only right which the complainant acquires is the remedy for breach of contract in a civil court.
Mere breach of contract cannot give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown at the beginning of the transaction.

In S.W. Palanitkar & Ors. vs. State of Bihar & Anr. (2002) 1 SCC 241, this Court held as under:
"21 ......In order to constitute an offence of cheating, the intention to deceive should be in existence at the time when the inducement was made.

sentences.text: It is necessary to show that a person had fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time of making the promise, to say that he committed an act of cheating.
A mere failure to keep up promise subsequently cannot be presumed as an act leading to cheating."

The above view in Palanitkar's case was referred to and followed in Rashmi Jain vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr. (2014) 13 SCC 553"
12.

sentences.text: A careful perusal of the FIR and the material collected during investigation reveals that the allegations do not disclose the existence of any fraudulent or dishonest intention at the inception of the transaction, which is a sine qua non for constituting an offence under Section 420 IPC.
Similarly, NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26030 6 MCRC-37168-2021 the ingredients of Section 467, 468, 471 of IPC are also not satisfied.

13. Upon consideration of the submissions made by learned counsel for the petitioners and on perusal of the record, it appears that the dispute raised in the FIR revolves around ownership and title of the property in question.

The documents placed on record, including resolutions, receipts,
and sale deeds, prima facie indicate that the petitioners derived title through lawful means from the original allottee, Anish Khan.

The complainant submitted an application on 14.06.2020 at Police Station Badoni, alleging that land measuring 30x30 sq. ft., situated at Mauja, Badoni within the jurisdiction of Nagar Panchayat Badoni, was allotted in the name of Vishvajeet Singh vide resolution dated 27.01.2009, along with a No Objection Certificate issued on the same date.

The accused persons, by adopting underhand means, executed a sale deed on 13.11.2019, wherein the present applicant showed himself as the seller and the co-accused as the purchasers, despite having no right or authority over the said land.

Based on this complaint, an FIR was registered at Crime No.
193/2020 for offences punishable under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the IPC.

The land in question infact allotted by the Village Panchayat Badoni Khurd, Datia, to one Anish Khan vide resolution dated 01.12.2004, who duly paid the premium amount and was issued an ownership certificate on 10.12.2004.

Anish Khan thereafter sold the land to petitioner no. 1 by a registered sale deed dated 25.02.2005, and petitioner no. 1 subsequently sold it to petitioner no. 2 through a registered sale deed dated 18.11.2019.

Even C.M.O. Nagar Parishad Badoni in his letter/notice dated 3.4.2021 had accepted that the NEUTRAL CITATION NO. 2025:MPHC-GWL:26030 7 MCRC-37168-2021 NOC issued in favour of petitioner no.1 was not forged rather was issued by him,
which also implies that there was no element of cheating involved and there was no use of any forged document.

The petitioners thus have a claim/title derived through a chain of lawful Azad Khan vs The State Of Madhya Pradesh on 8 October, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/21282029/

sentences.text: It is thus found that the FIR is based on false and baseless allegations and that the dispute, if any, is purely civil in nature but has been maliciously given a criminal colour to harass the petitioners.
There is no material in the FIR or accompanying documents to suggest any fraudulent or dishonest intention on the part of the petitioners at the time of executing the sale deeds.
The necessary ingredients of the offences under Sections 420, 467, 468, and 471 IPC are not made out.
The allegations, at best, indicate a civil dispute over title, which has been given a criminal colour.
14. On perusal of the FIR and the material collected during investigation, it is evident that the dispute thus falls squarely within the domain of a civil liability.

15. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in Satish Mehra v. State (N.C.T. of Delhi) and Another , AIR 2013 SC 506 , has held that the inherent powers of the High Court under Section 482 Cr.P.C. are wide and plenary in nature and may be exercised at any stage of criminal proceedings to prevent abuse of the process of law or to secure the ends of justice.

entities.text: Satish Mehra v. State (N.C.T. of Delhi) and Another , AIR 2013 SC 506
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It has been observed that where the allegations made in the FIR or complaint do not prima facie disclose the commission of a cognizable offence, the accused should not be compelled to undergo the rigours of a protracted criminal trial.

16. In the present case, even if the entire allegations in the FIR are NEUTRAL CITATION NO.
2025:MPHC-GWL:26030 8 MCRC-37168-2021 taken at their face value, they merely disclose a civil dispute.
The initiation of criminal proceedings appears to be a device to settle personal scores.
Continuance of such prosecution would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court.

17. Accordingly, this Court is of the considered view that the FIR bearing Crime No.193/2020 registered at Police Station Badoni, District Datia, for offences punishable under Sections 420, 467,
468, 471 of IPC against the petitioners and all consequential proceedings arising therefrom, deserve to be and are hereby quashed.
18. The petition is accordingly allowed.
No order as to costs.

(MILIND RAMESH PHADKE) JUDGE (aspr)
